name: Socialism
summary: Socialism holds that the means of production should be socially owned and democratically controlled rather than held by a class of private owners, so that production serves human needs instead of profit. Socialists see capitalism as exploiting and dominating workers and as prone to crisis, and aim to abolish class divisions altogether. The tradition is internationalist, secular, democratic and egalitarian, and backs the labor movement, public provision of services and progressive taxation along the way.
scope: The common core of the socialist family: social ownership of the means of production and a classless society, as set out in the classical programs of the labor movement (the SPD's 1891 Erfurt Program, Engels' Socialism: Utopian and Scientific) and a contemporary independent socialist party (Socialist Party USA's Statement of Principles), interpreted through the Stanford Encyclopedia's account. It excludes social democracy, which accepts capitalism, Leninist one-party communism, and anarchism, each audited separately, and leans on the family's mainstream where strands such as market and non-market socialists divide.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The classical socialist program demanded free medical care, medicine and midwifery for all, and socialists treat health as a need to be met socially rather than sold for profit.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Socialists back immediate labor protections that improve workers' lot under capitalism, though their aim is to end the wage system rather than adjust its floor.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Socialists argue that capitalist markets produce an 'anarchy of production', recurring crises and unmet needs, and that social control of production serves needs better.

public-ownership.rationale: Social ownership of land, mines, transport and other means of production is the defining aim of socialism.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The classical program demanded graduated income and property taxes and abolition of indirect taxes that burden workers, and socialists see concentrated wealth as the product of exploitation.

unions-good.rationale: The labor movement is the historical base of socialism, and its programs insist on freedom of association and workers' organization.

property-fundamental.rationale: Socialists reject private ownership of the means of production as the root of class domination and want it replaced by social property, so they deny it is a near-inviolable right.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Until production is socialized, socialists demand strict state inspection, working-hour limits and other controls on capitalist firms, whose power they see as domination.

cut-welfare.rationale: Socialists see poverty as a product of capitalism, not of welfare, and demand expanded free public provision; cutting it is the opposite of their program.

worker-ownership.rationale: Many socialists hold that workers should control the means of production they use, and contemporary socialist programs call for worker and community cooperatives.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Inferred from socialists' long record as targets of state repression and their demands for full civil liberties; security arguments for surveillance are viewed with suspicion.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Inferred from contemporary socialists' emphasis on bodily autonomy and opposition to punitive policing; historically the movement did not take a clear stand.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Socialists are split: the classical program demanded repeal of all restrictions on expression, while many modern socialists support curbs on racist and bigoted speech.

strong-leader.rationale: Mainstream socialists hold that socialism and democracy are inseparable and reject authoritarian rule; a leader bypassing democratic institutions contradicts 'democracy from below'.

state-harmful.rationale: Socialists use the state to socialize production and hold it is not inherently harmful, though Marxists expect it to die out once classes are abolished.

limit-guns.rationale: Classical socialists wanted an armed citizen militia in place of a standing army, while modern socialists stress anti-militarism; there is no settled view on private gun control.

empower-police-military.rationale: Socialists condemn militarism and preparation for war and wanted a people's militia to replace the standing army; they see police and military as guarding the existing class order.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Socialists have long seen prostitution as a product of poverty and capitalism, but modern socialist feminists are divided between decriminalization and abolition.

decide-locally.rationale: Socialist programs call for self-government at every level and community control of neighborhoods and schools, alongside planning at regional and national levels.

rehabilitation.rationale: The classical program demanded abolition of capital punishment and compensation for the wrongly convicted, and socialists attribute much crime to social conditions rather than individual wickedness.

traditional-family.rationale: Socialists seek to abolish male supremacy and all laws that disadvantage women, and see the patriarchal family as shaped by property relations rather than as society's foundation.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Contemporary socialist programs oppose homophobia and affirm people's right to determine their own sexual orientation, which implies full marriage equality.

abortion-legal.rationale: Contemporary socialist programs explicitly demand safe, legal abortion at no cost as part of people's control over their own bodies.

more-religion-public.rationale: Socialists hold that religion is a private matter, demanding an end to public funding of churches and secular schools.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Socialists oppose exploitation based on race and contemporary programs back expanded affirmative action, arguing racism will not disappear on its own.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Inferred from socialist feminism, which treats women's subordination as historically produced rather than natural; adherents differ on how far gender itself is constructed.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Socialism is internationalist, holding that workers everywhere have more in common with each other than with their own rulers, so national tradition carries little weight.

gradual-change.rationale: Socialists seek a fundamental transformation of property relations; even reformist socialists see existing institutions as instruments of class rule rather than things to respect.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Socialist internationalism aligns with working people of all countries rather than any nation, and contemporary socialists organize in solidarity with immigrants.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Inferred from the socialist demand for international arbitration of disputes and internationalism, tempered by suspicion of bodies run by capitalist states.

free-trade.rationale: Socialists reject the claim that capitalist market exchange benefits everyone, seeing it as enriching owners while exposing workers to competition and crisis.

nation-first.rationale: Socialism is explicitly internationalist, declaring workers' interests the same in every country and aligning with no nation.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Socialists condemn war and imperialism and typically see interventions by capitalist powers as serving imperial interests, though some accept specific cases.

open-borders.rationale: Inferred from proletarian internationalism and the solidarity of workers across countries; few socialist programs state open borders explicitly.

limit-growth.rationale: Classical socialism aimed to unleash productive forces, while many contemporary socialists put ecological limits first; the family is genuinely split.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Socialists want production planned in harmony with the natural environment and blame profit-driven production for ecological harm, favoring sweeping collective action.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Socialists hold that technology helps only once society controls production; under capitalism it can deepen crises and domination, so technology alone is not the answer.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Some contemporary socialist programs call for a 'nuclear-free world', though classical productivist socialists had no such objection.

revolution-justified.rationale: Socialists hold that a fundamental, revolutionary change in economic and political relations is needed, and the tradition defends revolutions against class rule.

experts-over-public.rationale: Socialists favor radical democracy from below and distrust rule by a bureaucratic or managerial layer over working people.

central-planning.rationale: Socialists argue that production planned by society can avoid capitalism's crises, though market socialists and critics of Soviet planning dissent.

socialized-markets.rationale: Market socialism, in which firms are worker- or publicly owned but trade in markets, is a major strand; non-market socialists consider it insufficient.

land-value-tax.rationale: Socialists want land made social property rather than left private and taxed, so they treat a single land tax as an inadequate reform.

tax-inheritance.rationale: The classical socialist program explicitly demanded a graduated inheritance tax by size of estate.

basic-income.rationale: Socialists are divided: some see unconditional basic income as a step toward freedom from wage labor, others as a subsidy to capitalism that substitutes for social ownership.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: The classical program demanded abolition of customs duties that serve the privileged at the expense of the majority, and socialists see protection as aiding domestic capitalists.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Socialists want society, not private owners, to decide what is produced and invested, which in practice means public direction of investment.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Socialists see concentration destroying small business as inevitable and answer it with social property, not by restoring small proprietors.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Classical socialism expects commodity production and wage labor to end under social ownership, but market socialists keep money and wages.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Socialists want society to control finance and the economy more, not hand money over to unregulated markets.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Socialists aim to abolish the class division between employers and workers rather than institutionalize collaboration between them under the state.

one-party-rule.rationale: Mainstream socialists oppose authoritarian statist regimes and support a multi-party system; one-party rule belongs to the Leninist strand this profile excludes.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Socialists seek to abolish all class privilege and hereditary rule, demanding that officials be elected by and accountable to the people.

democracy-best.rationale: Socialists hold that socialism and democracy are indivisible and have fought for universal, equal suffrage.

direct-votes.rationale: The classical program demanded that the people be able to propose and reject laws directly, alongside elected assemblies.

workers-councils.rationale: Council and syndicalist socialists put workers' councils first, while parliamentary socialists work through elected legislatures; the family is split.

right-to-secede.rationale: Inferred from the socialist support for national self-determination and opposition to imperialism, though socialists prefer unity of workers across borders.

natural-rulers.rationale: Socialism aims to abolish classes and class rule entirely and rejects any natural hierarchy among people.

political-violence-never.rationale: Socialists favor non-violent direct action but defend self-defense and revolution against class rule, so they reject an absolute ban.

war-builds-character.rationale: Socialists condemn war, preparation for war and militaristic culture.

separate-church-state.rationale: The classical program declared religion a private matter, ended public funding of churches and secularized schools.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Socialists want religion kept a private matter and law grounded in secular democratic decisions.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Socialists want justice free and administered by elected judges, and oppose turning public functions into private profit.

military-superiority.rationale: Socialists oppose militarism and imperial rivalry, favoring arbitration and solidarity across borders.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Socialists oppose exploitation by race and align with working people of every nation rather than an ethnic community.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The Marxian core of the socialist tradition holds that history is driven by changes in production and the struggles of classes; ethical and religious socialists put it less strongly.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Socialists aim at a classless society distributing according to need, going beyond formal opportunity, though many accept some unequal reward.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Inferred from contemporary socialist anti-imperialism and opposition to oppression of colonized peoples; classical socialism did not address it.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Inferred from socialist anti-imperialism; programs rarely state reparations explicitly.

civilizational-union.rationale: Socialists unite workers across all religions and civilizations and treat religion as private, opposing unions based on faith or civilization.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Socialists value community, solidarity and cooperation and criticize the profit motive, though they also value individual self-realization.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Socialists stress solidarity and community but also individual freedom and civil liberties, so they do not rank duties over rights.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Classical socialists saw nature as a resource for human needs, while ecological socialists ascribe it value in itself; the family is divided.

limit-population.rationale: Inferred from the socialist view that poverty stems from how production is organized, not from population; Marxists historically rejected Malthusian arguments.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Socialists see industrial productive forces as the basis for ending scarcity and class society once they are socially controlled.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Socialists welcome developing productive forces but want them under social control rather than disrupting workers' lives for profit; positions vary.

human-enhancement.rationale: Socialists support bodily autonomy but worry about unequal access to enhancement under capitalism; there is no settled position.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Inferred from the socialist commitment to democratic control from below, which sits uneasily with handing decisions to opaque systems.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Inferred from socialists' demand for full civil liberties and their experience as targets of state surveillance.

restore-past-order.rationale: Socialism looks forward to a classless society beyond capitalism rather than back to a lost order.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Socialists judge policy by whether it moves toward social ownership and away from class rule, and suspect 'pragmatism' of accepting capitalism as given.

direct-action.rationale: Socialists fought for universal suffrage and run candidates independent of capitalist parties, while also backing strikes and nonviolent direct action, so they combine the two rather than give up on elections.

means-match-ends.rationale: Contemporary socialists hold that the process of struggle shapes the ends achieved and that socialism and democracy are indivisible, so they insist on democratic, nonviolent means.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Socialists see developed industrial productive forces as the basis for ending scarcity and class society, the opposite of a return to foraging.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Marxian non-market socialists look to overcoming the old division of labor and the split between mental and manual work, while market socialists keep ordinary specialization; inferred from these strands' differing visions.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Socialists treat meeting needs as the aim of production and many hold distribution by need as the ultimate ideal, though market socialists would reward work in the meantime.

production-for-use.rationale: Production for human needs rather than private profit is the defining socialist goal, stated in the classical and contemporary programs alike.

profit-exploitation.rationale: The socialist critique of capitalism holds that owners' profit is surplus value taken from the workers whose labor produces it.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Mainstream socialists reject authoritarian statist regimes and hold socialism and democracy to be indivisible; the dictatorship of the proletariat belongs to the Leninist strand this profile excludes.

collective-farming.rationale: The classical program sought social ownership of land, but socialists long preferred voluntary cooperatives to forcing peasants off their farms; inferred from the general demand for social ownership.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Socialists tie militarism and imperialism to capitalism, which they say sets workers to fight other workers, though not every strand holds great-power war to be inevitable.

taxation-theft.rationale: Socialists demand graduated income and property taxes to fund public provision and treat taxation as a legitimate tool of social justice.

harm-principle.rationale: Socialists defend personal liberty and privacy, but they want the state to secure needs and control production well beyond preventing harm; inferred from their programs.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Socialists cherish personal rights but also assert collective rights of workers, unions and oppressed groups, and analyze society in terms of classes rather than isolated individuals.

conscription.rationale: The classical program called for universal training in arms and a people's militia, while contemporary socialists condemn militarism and preparation for war; the tradition is split.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Socialists put democratic control at the heart of their program, so voice, not leaving, is the check they want on power.

state-as-business.rationale: Socialists want public institutions run democratically for social needs, not on the model of profit-making firms serving customers.

media-academia-power.rationale: Socialists locate real power with the owners of capital, who they see as controlling the media too; inferred from their class analysis.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Socialists fight racism as a social system rooted in oppression rather than nature; inferred from their egalitarianism and anti-racist programs.

organic-representation.rationale: Socialists demand universal suffrage with proportional representation and run their own parties, though some favor workplace councils alongside them.

total-state.rationale: Mainstream socialists reject authoritarian statist regimes and defend civil liberties, privacy and cultural diversity against state control.

national-rebirth.rationale: Socialism is explicitly internationalist and frames politics in terms of class, not of a nation's decadence or renewal.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Socialists condemn imperialism, war and preparation for war, and call for international arbitration of disputes.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Socialists want all officials elected and accountable to the people and seek to abolish hereditary and class privilege.

bound-labor.rationale: Socialists see serfdom as an earlier form of class exploitation and aim to abolish all class domination of laborers.

knowledge-power.rationale: The Marxian strand holds that dominant ideas reflect the interests of the ruling class, though it also claims a scientific basis for socialism; inferred from that ideology critique.

universal-morality.rationale: Ethical socialists ground socialism in universal values such as equality and freedom, while many Marxists treat morality as historically conditioned; the family is split.

single-common-good.rationale: Socialists want society to plan production for the common good of a classless society rather than broker between class interests; inferred from their critique of capitalism's anarchy of production.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Inferred from socialist internationalism and its rejection of nationalism; Labor Zionism was a socialist current that disagreed, so the family is not uniform.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Socialists favor free movement of workers but reject citizenship based on nationality; inferred from internationalism, with no settled position on diaspora return.

revive-national-language.rationale: Socialist programs say nothing on reviving languages; inferred from their indifference to national culture as a political aim, alongside support for cultural diversity.

missingStatements.text: Profit made from owning businesses comes from exploiting the workers who produce it.
missingStatements.rationale: The claim that capitalist profit is surplus taken from workers is central to the socialist critique of capitalism.

missingStatements.text: Goods and services should be produced to meet people's needs rather than to make a profit.
missingStatements.rationale: Production for use, not profit, is the defining aim stated in socialist programs and theory.

notes: Socialism is an umbrella; strands answer differently. Market socialists accept money, wages and markets; non-market and council socialists would answer abolish-money-wages and workers-councils at +2. Leninists would back one-party rule and vanguard leadership; ecosocialists would take limit-growth and nature-intrinsic-value positively; classical productivist socialists would favor nuclear power and technology. Positions on contemporary social issues (abortion, LGBT rights, drugs) rely on modern socialist parties rather than the classical texts.
